summary: How to render a 250-mile driving-distance reachable-area polygon from home, EV-aware, in Leaflet

result.hosted:
## Bottom line

**Target: ~250 mi = 402 km = 402,336 m of driving distance.** Only three hosted services clear that bar. Two of them are EV-native.

| Service | Distance-contour hard cap | Time cap (drive) | Clears 402 km? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HERE Isoline Routing v8** | **1,000,000 m** (1000 km / 621 mi) | 32,400 s (9 h) | **YES** (2.5× headroom) |
| **HERE `range[type]=consumption`** | **650,000 Wh**, dynamic cap ≈900 km of travel | — | **YES — EV-native** |
| **TravelTime `/distance-map`** | **800,000 m** (800 km / 497 mi) | — | **YES** |
| **ABRP/Iternio `POST /range`** | no distance cap — driven by SoC | — | **YES — EV-native** |
| TravelTime `/time-map` | — | 14,400 s (4 h) | time variant only |
| ORS public `/v2/isochrones` | **120 km** (74.6 mi) | **1 h** | **NO — 3.4× short** |
| ORS self-hosted | config default 50,000 m, unbounded | default 18,000 s | yes, if self-hosted |
| Mapbox Isochrone | **100,000 m** (100 km / 62 mi) | 60 min | **NO — 4× short** |
| GraphHopper hosted | not published (time caps only) | **60 min even on Custom** | **NO** as published |
| GraphHopper self-hosted (OSS) | `distance_limit` meters, no documented cap | none | yes, if self-hosted |
| Google Isochrones API (Preview) | **no distance option at all** | **3,600 s DRIVE** | **NO** |

## Two hard blockers that kill services independently of the numbers

**Mapbox — Leaflet is a ToS violation.** Verbatim from the Isochrone API docs restrictions section: *"Results must be displayed on a Mapbox map using one of the Mapbox libraries or SDKs."* Vanilla-JS-plus-vendored-Leaflet is exactly the disallowed case. Mapbox is disqualified twice over (100 km cap AND the display clause).

**Google — same problem, plus no distance mode.** Google Maps Platform ToS §3.2.3(e) "No Use With Non-Google Maps": *"Customer will not use the Google Maps Core Services with or near a non-Google Map in a Customer Application."* Google does now ship a dedicated **Isochrones API** (`POST https://isochrones.googleapis.com/v1/isochrones:generate`), new since your last look — but it is **Preview**, **time-only** (`travelDuration`, no distance field), **capped at 3,600 s for `DRIVE`** (7,200 s other modes), and returns **one isochrone per request** (no multi-contour). Free 10,000 req/mo, then $3.00/1k, 600 req/min per project. Dead for the headline feature on all three counts.

## Per-service detail

### HERE Isoline Routing v8 — the strongest hosted fit
Straight from HERE's own OpenAPI spec (`GET https://isoline.router.hereapi.com/v8/openapi`, spec version **8.47.1**), `Range.type`:
```
- `distance` with units in meters with maximum value 1000000
- `time` with units in seconds with maximum value 32400
- `consumption` For fuel-based Vehicles : Static maximum value of 40000 ...
                For EV : Maximum value of 650000 with units in Watt-hours (Wh).
                Dynamic limit up to the maximum value that allows the vehicle to
                travel a maximum of 900kms.
```
The consumption mode is the one you actually want. It takes an EV consumption model directly:
```
range[type]=consumption&range[values]=<Wh available>
ev[freeFlowSpeedTable]=...   # Wh/m vs speed
ev[trafficSpeedTable]=...
ev[ascent]=9&ev[descent]=4.3 # Wh/m climbed / recovered
ev[auxiliaryConsumption]=1.8
```
`ev[ascent]` / `ev[descent]` are what make the Front Range asymmetry fall out physically rather than as a routing-speed artifact. You'd feed it your measured Wh/mi converted to a Wh/m speed table and your current usable pack Wh. Multi-range is supported (`range[values]=a,b,c`) so a 3-ring "0% / 10% / 20% reserve" render is one call. `routingMode=short|fast`, `shape[maxPoints]` (use >100 for quality), `optimizeFor` for speed/quality tradeoff.

Caveat HERE states itself: *"The isolines are not guaranteed to be 100% accurate… the returned polygons may contain points that are not reachable and may miss points that are reachable."*

**Pricing — partially unverifiable.** I could confirm from HERE's own page that the **Limited Plan** (no payment info on file) is **1,000 requests/day total** with **Isoline Routing at 1 RPS**. I could **not** verify the current Base Plan monthly free allowance — here.com/get-started/pricing is fully JS-rendered and third-party trackers disagree wildly (one says 250k transactions/mo, another says 5k/mo). Do not quote a number here; check the signup page. 1,000/day is plenty for a solar-charge-tracking refresh loop regardless.

### TravelTime — clears the distance bar, and it's what your screenshot is
`POST https://api.traveltimeapp.com/v4/distance-map`, field `travel_distance`: *"Maximum journey distance (in meters). Maximum value is **800000 (800km)** as standard. Minimum value is 75 meters. Although travel distance is limited, computations are still performed by considering fastest journeys (minimizing travel time)."* That last sentence matters — it's a fastest-route-constrained-by-distance shape, which is the highway-lobe look you want, not a shortest-path blob.

`/time-map` (isochrone) caps at **14,400 s (4 h)** — fine for a "reachable in 30 min" variant.

**Screenshot ID — confirmed.** TravelTime's own web app at `app.traveltime.com` ships a button with `aria-label="Add shape"` and CSS class `addShapeTab` (found in its JS bundle `070-u4-bin-me.js`). TravelTime calls isochrones "shapes" throughout their API docs too (`unions`, "shapes to be unioned"). Your reference image is TravelTime's app with near-certainty.

**Limits/pricing.** Free trial = 2 weeks at 60 hits/min; after expiry a **"Free Restricted" plan at 5 hits/min**. A hit = 1 isochrone. Critically for visual quality: `level_of_detail` is capped at **Medium (0)** on Trial, Unlimited, and Free Restricted plans; only **Custom** plans get **Highest (2)**. At an 800 km shape, Medium detail will be noticeably coarse — you will not get Tesla-grade lobe/hole fidelity on a free key. Max 10 searches and 10 unions per request. **Pricing is not published** — TravelTime markets "anti-usage-based pricing… fixed price" and routes everything to sales. I cannot quote a figure.

### ABRP / Iternio — there IS a reachable-area endpoint, and it's exactly this feature
Undocumented in the public marketing pages but present in the live spec at `https://api.iternio.com/swagger-ui/spec/prod/IternioPlanning.out.yaml`:

```yaml
/range:
  post:
    summary: (alpha) Create a range plot
    description: Create a range plot showing reachable points from a given
                 location based on vehicle and conditions.
```
`RangeRequest` takes:
- `vehicle` → `currentSocFrac`, **`referenceConsumption` ([Wh/km @ 110 km/h], 0–1000)**, `degradationFrac`, `configuration`
- `currentLocation`, `speed`, `avoid`, **`traffic`**, **`weather`**
- **`soc`**: array of SoC reserve levels (default `[0.2, 0.05, 0]`, max 10) — **one polygon per reserve level**
- `radialsCount`: 8–256, default 32

Response `RangeOk` = `{ranges: [GeoJSON Feature<Polygon> with properties.soc]}` — straight into Leaflet's `L.geoJSON`, no conversion. This is the only service that takes your measured Wh/km and battery state as first-class inputs and hands back reserve-banded polygons.

**Two real caveats.** (1) `radialsCount` means it's **radial sampling** — up to 256 rays from home, polygon = the endpoints. That gives a star-ish polygon; it will **not** produce the concave lobes and interior holes of a true graph-expansion isochrone. At 32 (default) it will look crude; at 256 it's better but still fundamentally star-shaped. (2) It is marked **alpha** and tagged `development`. (3) Access: `ApiKeyAuth`, and ABRP's own API page says *"Setup costs and per-plan pricing vary based on your integration needs and usage volume"* — no published price, no self-serve tier, and no statement that individuals are eligible. Telemetry-only keys are free; **Planning API keys are not**. The free Telemetry API does not expose `/range`.

### OpenRouteService — disqualified for headline, viable for the time variant
Public API restrictions page states for isochrones: **Locations 5, Intervals 10, Range distance 120 km, Range time (Driving profiles) 1 h.** Rate limits: **500 isochrones/day, 20/min** on the free key; the Collaborative plan (humanitarian/academic/gov, application required) gives 2,500/day, 40/min. 120 km is 30% of what you need — dead for 250 mi. Fine for "reachable in 30/45/60 min" with up to 10 nested rings in one call, and unlike Mapbox/Google there is **no basemap restriction** (OSM/ODbL, attribution only), so it's legal on Leaflet.

**Self-host** removes the cap: `ors.endpoints.isochrones.maximum_range_distance_default` (default 50,000 m), `maximum_range_time_default` (18,000 s), `maximum_locations` (2), `maximum_intervals` (1) — all raisable per-profile, plus a `fastisochrones` section with its own limits. Runs in Docker on the Mac, but you'd need an OSM extract covering a 250 mi radius from Longmont (CO + WY + NE + KS + NM panhandles) and the RAM to graph-build it.

### GraphHopper — disqualified as hosted
Pricing matrix publishes **only a time cap**, and only on paid tiers: **Basic €69/mo → 15 min; Standard €199/mo → 20 min; Premium €479/mo → 30 min; Custom → up to 60 min.** The **Free** row (€0, 500 credits/day, non-commercial use only — which fits your project) shows **no value at all** in the "Isochrone API max. time" cell, so free-tier isochrone availability is ambiguous; treat as unavailable until tested. Rate limits: Premium 10 req/s + 1000 credits/min, Standard 2 req/s + 400 c/min, Basic 1 req/s + 100 c/min. **The per-request credit cost for isochrones is not published** on the pricing page (it links a "Credit cost details" page). **No distance cap is published anywhere I could find** — only time — so I can't give you a number for `distance_limit` on the hosted API. Even at the most generous read, 60 min of driving ≈ 70 mi, so hosted GraphHopper is out.

**Self-host (OSS)** has no such caps: `GET /isochrone?profile=car&distance_limit=<meters>&buckets=N` (`distance_limit` default -1 = off, `time_limit` default 600 s), plus `/spt` for a raw reachable-point list instead of a polygon. Same OSM-extract/RAM tradeoff as ORS.

## What this means for the terrain-asymmetry point

Only **HERE consumption isolines** and **ABRP `/range`** model energy. Every other option on this list computes a *distance* or *time* contour, in which the Rockies show up only as low road density and slow speeds — the shape will bulge east and pinch west, but for the wrong reason, and it won't respond to grade at all. A 6% grade costing ~2× the Wh/mi is invisible to Mapbox/ORS/GraphHopper/TravelTime/Google. If the terrain asymmetry is the visual point of the feature, HERE's `range[type]=consumption` with `ev[ascent]`/`ev[descent]` is the only hosted API that produces it correctly *and* clears 402 km *and* is legal on Leaflet.

## Refresh-rate math for the solar-charging animation

One SoC update = one request. 5-minute polling over a 10-hour solar day ≈ 120 requests/day; 1-minute ≈ 600/day.
- HERE Limited Plan: 1,000/day, Isoline 1 RPS → fits, but you're near the ceiling at 1-min polling.
- TravelTime post-trial: 5 hits/min → fits any sane polling rate.
- ORS free: 500/day, 20/min → fits (time variant only).
- Mapbox: 100,000/mo free, then $2.00/1k → numerically trivial, but ToS-blocked.
- Google: 10,000/mo free (600 req/min) → fits, but 60-min cap and ToS-blocked.

## Explicitly not verified

- **HERE Base Plan monthly free allowance.** Page is JS-rendered; third-party sources contradict each other. Only the Limited Plan figure (1,000 req/day) came from HERE's own page.
- **TravelTime pricing.** Not published; sales-gated.
- **ABRP Planning API pricing and individual eligibility.** Not published; "setup costs… vary."
- **GraphHopper's isochrone `distance_limit` cap and per-request credit cost.** Neither appears on the pricing page or the OpenAPI reference.

Scratchpad artifacts (raw evidence): `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-d-Code-tesla-automation/677157a0-46bb-4378-8526-f607ae31840c/scratchpad/here_openapi.yml` (HERE spec 8.47.1), `.../abrp.yaml` (Iternio Planning API spec), `.../here_ref.md`.

result.selfhost:
## Recommendation: roll it yourself. Not because the engines can't — because they compute the wrong quantity.

I verified the engine limits, then benchmarked the DIY path. The DIY path won by more than I expected.

---

## 1. Verified engine facts

### Valhalla — can do 250 mi, one config line, but wrong metric

Exact defaults from `scripts/valhalla_build_config` (`service_limits.isochrone`):

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `max_contours` | `4` | max contour objects per request |
| `max_time_contour` | `120` | **minutes** |
| `max_distance_contour` | `200` | **kilometres** = 124.3 mi ← **the actual cap** |
| `max_locations` | `1` | |
| `max_distance` | `25000.0` | metres — **inert here**, see below |

You need 402 km, so **the default caps you at less than half**. Fix is one line: `max_distance_contour: 450`. Exceeding it throws error 166 (`src/loki/isochrone_action.cc`).

**`max_distance: 25000` is a red herring** — widely misread as a radius cap. Its description is *"Maximum b-line distance between all **locations**"*, and `check_distance()` loops `for source in [begin, end-1)`. With `max_locations: 1` the loop body never executes. It cannot constrain a single-origin isochrone.

**Three defaults will sabotage the visual** if left alone:
- `polygons` defaults to **`false`** → you get LineStrings, which won't fill in Leaflet. Set `true`.
- `denoise` defaults to **`1`** → shows *only the largest contour*, deleting exactly the islands/lobes you're after. Set ~0.1.
- `generalize` defaults to `tilesize × 0.25 × mPerDegLat` = **138 m** at this scale.

**Raster is fine.** `grid_size = dlat/300` clamped to `[0.001, 0.005]`; at 402 km it pins to 0.005° → **1491 × 1938 = 2.89 M cells ≈ 23 MB**, cells 553 × 425 m. Not a scaling problem.

**macOS/Apple Silicon:** `ghcr.io/valhalla/valhalla:latest` ships **native `linux/arm64`** (verified via registry manifest) — no QEMU. Docker 28.1.1 already installed.

**Disk:** the six PBFs are **939.2 MB** (measured: CO 359.1, UT 158.8, NM 129.3, KS 108.9, NE 94.8, WY 88.3). Tiles typically land ~1.5–2.5× PBF, so ~2 GB, plus ~60 MB elevation. Fine against your 42 GiB free — *but that free space is the real ceiling; don't extrapolate to a US build.* Build time on an M1 Pro is roughly 30–90 min (estimate — I didn't build). Watch Docker Desktop's VM memory: default 8 GB is marginal for the enhancer stage on a 1 GB extract.

**The disqualifier — custom cost models:** `src/sif/autocost.cc` contains **zero** mentions of grade/elevation/hills. `bicyclecost.cc` has **38**. The tiles *do* carry `weighted_grade`, `max_up_slope`, `max_down_slope` per directed edge — the data is right there — but auto costing never reads it, and Valhalla has no scripting hook for costing. **An EV Wh/mi model means forking C++.**

So Valhalla gives you a gorgeous blob of *road distance*. That is not your feature.

### OSRM — no isochrone, and the workaround is worse than DIY

Six services: `nearest`, `route`, `table`, `match`, `trip`, `tile`. **No isochrone.** The folk technique is `table` (1 source × N grid points) then contour. Two problems: `max-table-size` defaults to **100** (`src/tools/routed.cpp`), and every grid point snaps to its nearest road — points in empty country snap to roads tens of km away and report nonsense. You'd be running a routing server to obtain data you can compute directly, then still writing the contouring yourself. Skip.

### pgRouting — the only one that can express your cost model off-the-shelf

`pgr_drivingDistance` returns **nodes with `agg_cost`, not a polygon**; you then apply `ST_ConcaveHull` (PostGIS 3.3+). Its genuine advantage: cost is just a **SQL column**, so a Wh formula with elevation is expressible without forking anything. Its cost: Postgres + PostGIS + pgRouting + an `osm2pgrouting` import that is slow and memory-hungry at multi-state scale — a database daemon bolted onto a project that currently uses SQLite. You'd take on all that to replace one 16 MB numpy array.

### openrouteservice — cap is liftable, RAM is the problem

From `ors-api/.../application.yml`: `maximum_range_distance_default: 50000`; driving-car override `100000`; **`fastisochrones` override `500000`** (500 km, which does clear your 402 km). Also `maximum_intervals: 1`, `maximum_locations: 2`. Self-hosted you can edit these anyway, so the cap was never the real barrier — the JVM plus CH **and** fastisochrones preprocessing for a 9-state graph on a 16 GB Mac is. And it still has no EV energy model.

---

## 2. The cheap approximation is not a compromise — it's the correct architecture

Your instinct is right, and it's stronger than you framed it. I benchmarked it.

**4 M nodes / 16 M directed edges (denser than a real road network), scipy CSR + Dijkstra:**

```
CSR build                 0.13 s
full Dijkstra             1.92 s      ← the "expensive" step
Dijkstra with cost cap    0.22 s
result array             16.0 MB float32
mmap load                15.4 ms
FILTER dist <= budget     2.6–3.0 ms  ← the per-render operation
```

**The Dijkstra is not the expensive part.** It's two seconds. The genuinely slow step is parsing OSM into a graph — done once.

**This changes the design in your favour.** Don't persist only `dist[]` — that locks you into one cost model forever. **Persist the CSR graph plus per-edge `(length, Δelevation)`.** Then re-solving for a *different* cost model (outside temperature, HVAC on, wheel/tyre choice, drive it hard) is ~2 seconds. You get live sliders, not a frozen table. Cache the current `dist[]` alongside it as the fast path.

**Round-trip for free.** Run a second Dijkstra on the *reversed* graph (with reversed grades). Two arrays, ~4 s total. Then:
- one-way reachable: `out[n] <= budget`
- there-and-back: `out[n] + back[n] <= budget`

These differ by far more than 2× in the mountains, because west is uphill and east is downhill. A toggle between them costs one extra array and is a genuinely honest feature.

**Graph size for the 250-mi circle** (from my Overpass measurements): ~414 k drivable ways → **~3.7 M geometry nodes**, or **~620 k** if simplified to intersections. At 12 B/node that's **7–45 MB**. Trivial.

**One warning:** at ~200 B/node of Python object overhead, networkx would cost ~0.74 GB and be orders of magnitude slower. **Use numpy CSR arrays, not networkx/osmnx graphs.** osmnx is fine as a one-time *importer*; it is the wrong runtime representation.

### Correction to your state list: it's 9 states, not 6

The 250-mi bbox is **36.528–43.806 N, −109.831 – −100.372 W**, which also intersects **South Dakota** (1.33° of overlap — the Black Hills, genuinely road-reachable via I-25→US-85), plus corners of **Oklahoma** and **Arizona** (those two are inside the box but *not* within 250 road-miles, so you can drop them). **Add South Dakota.** Better still: clip the extracts to the bbox with `osmium extract` — you don't need eastern Kansas or western Utah, and it cuts the parse substantially.

---

## 3. Elevation: this is what makes the feature true

Your instinct that ignoring 11,000 ft passes is "lying" is quantitatively correct. For a ~2100 kg Model S:

```
climb 1000 ft   = 2052 Wh      descend 1000 ft = −1038 Wh (70% regen)
Longmont (5,000 ft) → Loveland Pass (11,990 ft): +6,990 ft = 14.3 kWh
   ...on a ~100 kWh pack, that single climb is 14% of the battery.
```

A distance-based isochrone would put Loveland Pass and a point 60 miles east on the same contour. They are nowhere near equivalent.

**Cost model:** use your measured Wh/mi as the flat rolling+aero baseline (that's the whole point of collecting it), and *add* the physics grade term per edge:
`Wh_edge = measured_Wh_per_mi × miles + (m·g·Δh)/(3600·η)`, with regen recovery on descent.

**⚠️ The trap nobody mentions: descending edges produce negative Wh, and Dijkstra is invalid with negative weights.** It won't crash — it will silently return wrong distances. Bellman-Ford at this scale is far too slow.

**The clean fix:** clamp each edge to a positive floor justified by auxiliary load. The car draws 300–1000 W for HVAC/electronics regardless of grade, which at 60 mph is **5–17 Wh/mi**. Clamp `Wh_edge = max(Wh_edge, 8 × miles)`. This is physically defensible *and* restores Dijkstra's correctness. Elegant rather than a hack.

**Elevation source — verified no-auth:** AWS Terrain Tiles, `https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` returned **HTTP 200** with a valid 256×256 PNG. Decode: `elev_m = (R×256 + G + B/256) − 32768`. No login, no API key — unlike NASA Earthdata, which now requires an account. Zoom 10–12 is plenty; ~200 MB for your region. (CGIAR SRTM 90 m is a working fallback, also HTTP 200.)

---

## 4. Polygon complexity — measured, and it's a non-issue if you contour a raster

I built the full pipeline against a synthetic 201 k-point reachable cloud with realistic radial highways, a dense Front Range strip, sparse rural grid, and roadless mountain wilderness holes.

**Do not use alpha shapes.** A concave hull over 500 k points is slow, memory-hungry, and its parameter is unintuitive. **Rasterize and contour instead** — which is precisely what Valhalla itself does internally.

**The single most important aesthetic knob is the buffer radius**, and the spiderweb→blob transition is sharp:

| Buffer | Rings | Raw verts | After DP | After denoise | Area | GeoJSON |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 km | 354 | 167,940 | 3,746 | 86 rings / 2,620 v | 30.5% | 56 KB |
| **3.0 km** | 385 | 153,215 | 2,712 | **26 rings / 1,378 v** | 41.6% | **30 KB** |
| 5.0 km | 4 | 15,796 | 786 | 3 rings / 784 v | 56.6% | 17 KB |

Below ~2.5 km you get a spiderweb (12,000+ rings); above ~5 km the islands merge into a boring disc. **2–3 km is the Tesla-blob sweet spot** — lobes along highways, holes over wilderness.

**Timing:** `distance_transform_edt` **105 ms once** and is reusable for *every* radius (thresholding is 1 ms) — vastly better than iterated `binary_closing`, which cost 508–1178 ms *per radius*. Contour 15–35 ms, Douglas-Peucker 15–90 ms. **Whole polygon pipeline ≈ 200 ms.**

**Leaflet:** Douglas-Peucker at one screen pixel of tolerance collapses **153,215 → 2,712 vertices, a 56× reduction with zero visible loss.** The reason it's so effective: contours of a boolean raster are axis-aligned staircases, which DP annihilates. At z=7 (the natural overview zoom — the 805 km blob spans 861 px) one pixel is **934 m**, so Valhalla's 138 m vertices are 6.8× finer than a pixel — pure waste.

Your vendored Leaflet 1.9.4 already helps: `_update` runs `_clipPoints() → _simplifyPoints() → _updatePath()`, so it clips to viewport *then* Douglas-Peuckers at `smoothFactor: 1`. But `_projectLatlngs` still runs over **every** input vertex on every pan/zoom, so input size matters. At ~1,400 vertices / 30 KB this is a non-issue. `L.Canvas` and `preferCanvas` are present in your copy — worth setting, though you won't need it at this vertex count.

Serve 2–3 pre-simplified LODs and swap on `zoomend` if you want to zoom in past z=9.

---

## 5. ODbL for a personal, non-distributed project

**You have essentially no obligations.** ODbL triggers on (a) *distributing* the database or a derivative, or (b) *publicly using* a Produced Work. A map rendered on your own Mac and never shared triggers neither.

- Your precomputed distance table **is** a Derivative Database. You may keep it privately forever with no share-alike obligation. Share-alike only bites if you distribute it.
- If you ever screenshot the blob publicly, add **"© OpenStreetMap contributors"** — that's the whole requirement. Put it in the Leaflet attribution control now and you're permanently done.

**The practical constraints are usage policies, not the licence:**
- **Bulk-extract from Geofabrik, never Overpass.** I hit Overpass rate limits repeatedly during this research; it's for small queries and explicitly not for bulk extraction.
- If you use `tile.openstreetmap.org` for basemap tiles, the OSMF Tile Usage Policy applies — set a real `User-Agent` and don't preload. For a single-user dashboard, occasional use is fine.

---

## 6. Recommendation

**Build it yourself. numpy + scipy + contourpy — three wheels, no build step, no daemon, no Docker.**

One-time build:
1. `osmium extract` the 7 relevant state PBFs to the bbox → filter to drivable highways.
2. Parse to CSR arrays; attach node elevations from AWS terrarium tiles.
3. Persist `nodes(lat, lon, elev)` + CSR `(indptr, indices, length_m, delta_elev)` as `.npy`.

Per solve (~2 s): compute `Wh` per edge from your measured Wh/mi + grade, **clamp to an 8 Wh/mi floor**, Dijkstra forward and reverse, cache both arrays.

Per render (~200 ms): `mask = wh <= usable_kWh` → rasterize at 500 m → EDT → threshold at 3 km → contour → DP at one screen pixel → drop rings under ~8 vertices → GeoJSON (~30 KB).

Solar charging makes `usable_kWh` rise, and the blob grows — a 3 ms filter plus a 200 ms re-contour. You can animate it.

**Simplest thing that works (do this first, one day):** the exact same pipeline with edge cost = **metres**, no elevation. You get the road-following blob with real lobes and holes immediately. # Reachable-Area Map — Reconciled Verdict

*Synthesis of Report A (hosted APIs) and Report B (self-hosted/DIY), checked against the actual repo at `/Users/d/Code/tesla_automation`.*

**The two reports never evaluated each other's best option.** A never looked at Valhalla or DIY; B never looked at HERE. That single gap is the whole reconciliation: A's winner is cheaper, faster to ship, *and* more physically correct than B's winner — for v1. B's winner is right eventually, for reasons that have nothing to do with accuracy.

---

## 1. VERDICT TABLE

| Option | Hard distance cap | Setup cost | Running cost | Verdict — one-line reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HERE Isoline v8 `range[type]=consumption`** | 650,000 Wh, dynamic ≈900 km travel | ~50 lines Python, one API key, **zero new deps** (project already uses httpx) | **$0** — Limited Plan 1,000 req/day verified, 1 RPS | **VIABLE — PRIMARY.** Only option that clears 402 km, models grade energy natively, and is legal on Leaflet. |
| HERE Isoline v8 `range[type]=distance` | 1,000,000 m (621 mi) | same | $0 | **VIABLE — fallback only.** Clears the bar with 2.5× headroom but treats Loveland Pass as 60 flat miles. |
| **DIY numpy/scipy + Dijkstra + raster contour** | none | days: OSM parse pipeline, ~1 GB PBF, +numpy/scipy/contourpy into a 6-dep venv | **$0**, ~2 s/solve, ~200 ms/render, no third party | **VIABLE — v2 UPGRADE.** Correct destination, wrong starting point: buys control you have no inputs for yet. |
| TravelTime `/distance-map` | 800,000 m | moderate | **unpublished, sales-gated**; free-restricted 5 hits/min, `level_of_detail` capped at Medium | DISQUALIFIED — no published price, no self-serve, and Medium detail at 800 km will not give Tesla-grade lobes. |
| ABRP/Iternio `POST /range` | none (SoC-driven) | trivial | **unpublished; Planning keys are not free; alpha** | DISQUALIFIED **by the goal** — `radialsCount` ≤256 is radial sampling: a star, never concave lobes or holes. |
| Valhalla self-host (Docker) | 200 km default → `max_distance_contour: 450` | Docker + ~2 GB tiles + 30–90 min build | $0 | DISQUALIFIED for the stated feature — `sif/autocost.cc` has **zero** grade/elevation handling and no scripting hook. Energy = forking C++. |
| ORS hosted | **120 km** | trivial | $0, 500/day | DISQUALIFIED — 3.4× short. Fine for a "reachable in 45 min" side panel; legal on Leaflet (ODbL, attribution only). |
| ORS self-host | 500 km via `fastisochrones` | heaviest of all: JVM + CH + fastisochrones preprocessing, 9-state graph, 16 GB Mac | $0 | DISQUALIFIED — most RAM, and still no energy model. Worst of both worlds. |
| GraphHopper self-host | `distance_limit` unbounded | Docker + tile build | $0 | DISQUALIFIED — same as Valhalla: distance only, no EV model. |
| GraphHopper hosted | not published (time caps only) | trivial | Free tier's isochrone cell is **blank**; €69–479/mo buys 15–30 min | DISQUALIFIED — 60 min ≈ 70 mi even on Custom. |
| Mapbox Isochrone | **100,000 m** | trivial | $0 to 100k/mo | DISQUALIFIED **twice** — 4× short, and *"Results must be displayed on a Mapbox map"* forbids Leaflet. |
| Google Isochrones (Preview) | **no distance mode at all** | trivial | $0 to 10k/mo | DISQUALIFIED **three times** — time-only, 3,600 s DRIVE cap, and ToS §3.2.3(e) forbids non-Google maps. |
| OSRM | n/a — **no isochrone service** | — | — | DISQUALIFIED — the `table` workaround snaps empty-country points to roads tens of km away and you still write the contouring yourself. |
| pgRouting | none | Postgres + PostGIS + slow multi-state `osm2pgrouting` import | $0 + a database daemon | DISQUALIFIED — the only off-the-shelf tool that expresses Wh cost in SQL, but it's a DB server to replace one 16 MB numpy array in a SQLite project. |
| Naive circle at rated range | n/a | 5 lines | $0 | **KEEP — as an overlay.** Not the feature, but the best possible caption for it. See §4. |

---

## 2. THE RECOMMENDATION

**Ship HERE Isoline v8 in `consumption` mode. Put the DIY numpy engine behind the same HTTP interface as an earned v2, not a prerequisite.**

Why it beats the alternatives *for this deployment specifically*:

- **It fits the codebase's physical character.** The whole project is 4,100 lines and six dependencies. HERE adds one `httpx` call to `car_routes.py` and **zero** new packages. The DIY path adds numpy + scipy + contourpy (the venv at `/Users/d/Code/tesla_automation/.venv` currently has none of them) plus ~1 GB of PBF and a 200 MB terrain-tile cache, against **42 GiB free** — I checked. That's not disqualifying, but it's a different kind of project.
- **The terrain asymmetry — the stated visual point — works on day one.** This is the non-obvious part: HERE's `ev[ascent]`/`ev[descent]` are Wh-per-metre-climbed constants, which is *the same model* B derives from `(m·g·Δh)/(3600·η)`. The two reports converge on identical physics. So the grade term does not depend on having measured Wh/mi — only the overall *scale* does. **Your shape is right before your data exists.**
- **Cross-referencing the reports gives you the exact parameters.** B's physics (2,052 Wh per 1,000 ft climbed; 1,038 Wh recovered per 1,000 ft descended, for a ~2,100 kg Model S) converts directly into A's API fields: **`ev[ascent]=6.7`, `ev[descent]=3.4`** (Wh per metre). Neither report contains this line. It's the bridge.
- **The budget fits comfortably.** 78% SoC × ~95 kWh ≈ 74,100 Wh, against a 650,000 Wh cap and a 900 km dynamic travel limit. At ~0.186 Wh/m (300 Wh/mi) that's a ~400 km polygon — your 402 km target, with the cap nowhere in sight.
- **Cost is verified zero.** HERE's Limited Plan (no card on file) is 1,000 req/day, confirmed from HERE's own page. Every other hosted option with sufficient range has *unpublished, sales-gated* pricing (TravelTime, ABRP). "Free" beats "call sales" for a single-user hobby project.
- **Home never moves and the budget changes slowly.** Round the Wh budget into ~2 kWh buckets and cache on it. A 5-minute solar poll then triggers maybe 20 API calls/day, not 120 — the blob only redraws when it would visibly move.
- **The escape hatch is free.** Both engines emit GeoJSON Polygon/MultiPolygon per reserve level. Define `GET /car/reachable` once and the frontend never learns which engine drew it. Choosing HERE now costs nothing later.

**Cost of this choice, stated plainly:** home lat/lon and a battery-derived energy figure leave the Mac on every refresh. This is a personal telemetry dashboard with OAuth tokens on disk; that may or may not sit right with you. It is the one axis **neither report weighed**, and it is the only real argument for going DIY first.

---

## 3. STAGED PATH

**Ground truth on history: it is empty.** `car.db` holds 59 samples spanning **1.1 hours**, 8 distinct odometer values, ≈2 miles driven. Measured Wh/mi is weeks away. But `samples` already carries `odometer`, `battery_level`, `usable_battery_level`, `shift_state`, `outside_temp` — everything the v1.5 derivation needs. Nothing has to change in the schema.

### v1 — ships this week. Shape is honest; scale is explicitly provisional.

- `GET /car/reachable?reserve=0,10,20` in `/Users/d/Code/tesla_automation/car_routes.py` → one HERE call with `range[values]=` three Wh figures → three nested rings, one request.
- **Consumption input ladder, with the rung named in the response.** The car already reports two numbers, both already in the view model at `/Users/d/Code/tesla_automation/vehicle.py`: `range_mi` (rated — EPA constant × SoC; currently 262.61 @ 76% → ~345 mi at 100%) and `range_est_mi` (Tesla's own recent-consumption estimate). Neither is *your* measurement.
  - `provenance: "car-rated"` → the honest v1 label.
  - `provenance: "measured"` → not available; say so.
- **Draw two rings, not one.** The rated-derived edge and the est-derived edge, with the annulus between them **hatched**. That band *is* the uncertainty — the direct analogue of the dashed segments in `/Users/d/Code/tesla_automation/static/car.js:366`.
- **Overlay the naive circle** at rated range as a thin dashed reference. It costs five lines and it makes the entire feature legible: here is the lie, here is the road network, here is the mountain.
- **Freeze on stale data.** Reuse `GAP_SECONDS = 1800` from `/Users/d/Code/tesla_automation/store.py`. If the last SoC sample is older than that, the polygon must stop updating **and visibly say so** — not interpolate growth. See §4, item 8.
- **`#reach-note`** (the element already exists at `static/car.js:174`) states in one sentence: which consumption figure was used, that it assumes one-way travel with no charging, and when the SoC sample was taken.

### v1.5 — flips on automatically as data accrues. No new engine.

- Derive **pack usable kWh** from charge sessions: Δ`charge_energy_added` ÷ Δ`usable_battery_level`.
- Derive **measured Wh/mi** from driving segments only (`shift_state != 'P'`), pairing Δodometer against Δ(usable_soc × pack). **Energy-weight it; never average per-trip Wh/mi** — that's the same error `energy.py:summarize()` already documents itself refusing to make ("averaging per-day percentages would weight a cloudy 2 kWh day the same as a sunny 40 kWh one").
- **Gate the switchover and show the countdown.** Below threshold (suggest ~300 mi and ≥3 charge sessions), the note reads *"Measured Wh/mi: not yet — 47 of 300 mi."* That is the feature telling you what it doesn't know, in the codebase's own voice.
- Once measured, the hatched band stops being rated-vs-est and becomes **the observed p20–p80 spread of your own segments**. That's the version worth having: an empirical error bar.

### v2 — DIY engine, only if v1 earns it.

Swap the engine behind `/car/reachable`. Buys what HERE structurally cannot:
- **Round-trip toggle.** Forward + reverse Dijkstra, `out[n] + back[n] <= budget`. In the Front Range these differ by far more than 2×, because west is uphill and east is downhill. B is right that this is the genuinely honest mode, and it's ~4 s of compute.
- **Live sliders** — outside temp, HVAC, speed — each a ~2 s re-solve because you persisted the CSR graph and per-edge `(length, Δelev)`, not a frozen `dist[]`.
- **No third party, works offline.**

**Do not build v2 before v1.5 has data.** A precision instrument with no calibration is not precise.

### v3 — probably never
Per-edge elevation refinement, multiple pre-simplified LODs on `zoomend`. B's measurements say you won't need LODs: ~1,400 vertices / 30 KB after Douglas-Peucker at one screen pixel.

---

## 4. THE HONESTY PROBLEM

**The magnitude of the lie, concretely.** Longmont (~5,000 ft) → Loveland Pass (11,990 ft) is ~75 road miles. Flat model at 300 Wh/mi: 22.5 kWh. Reality: 22.5 + 14.3 (climb) = **36.8 kWh — 63% more.** A single-average-Wh/mi isochrone overstates westward reach by roughly 1.6× at the pass while being approximately right eastbound. The error is not noise; it is *signed and directional*, which is exactly the kind that reads as confidence.

### What the feature must NOT claim

1. **Not "you can get here."** It's *"roads inside this area are within budget, one-way, no charging stop, from this SoC sample."* Say all four qualifiers.
2. **Not a hard boundary.** HERE's own words: *"the returned polygons may contain points that are not reachable and may miss points that are reachable."* The edge is the **least** trustworthy pixel in the picture and must never be a crisp 2px line. Hatch it, feather it, or draw two.
3. **Not "your average Wh/mi applies here."** It does not apply on westbound I-70 in January at 70 mph with the cabin at 72°F. If a single scalar is driving the polygon, the note must say so.
4. **Not free energy on descent.** B's trap is real and silent: negative edge weights make Dijkstra return wrong answers without erroring. The 8 Wh/mi floor (justified by 300–1000 W of auxiliary draw) is physics, not a hack. Applies to v2; HERE presumably handles it internally, which is one more argument for v1.
5. **Not SoC = usable energy.** There's buffer below 0%, cold-battery unavailable capacity, and arriving at 0% is not a plan. Default the headline ring to the **20% reserve** band, not the 0% one, and label the 0% ring *"empty on arrival."*
6. **No false precision.** No "247.3 mi." Round to 10 mi. A number with a decimal point is a claim about the decimal point.
7. **Attribute the shape.** v1's polygon is HERE's opinion, v2's is yours. The note should say which. Basemap attribution is already correct in `static/car.js:190`.
8. **Never animate across a gap.** This is where the solar-growth feature will violate house style. The car sleeps; SoC samples stop; the blob must **freeze and be visibly marked stale** — greyed fill, note reading *"last SoC sample 2h 14m ago — not updating."* Interpolating growth from a charging *rate* while the car is asleep is precisely the invented slope that `store.py`'s `GAP_SECONDS` exists to refuse. The dashed line across gaps in the SoC chart is the precedent; a frozen, greyed polygon is its spatial equivalent.

### Presentation pattern that matches the house

`energy.py:money()` returns `None` and the UI hides the row when rates aren't set in `.env` — *"Only shown when the user actually set rates."* Same rule here: **when provenance is weak, show the provenance instead of the number.** v1 shows a shape and a caveat, not "254 miles."

---

## 5. CONCRETE FIRST STEP

**One curl and one throwaway HTML file. ~1 hour including signup. It proves or kills the primary recommendation outright.**

1. **(~15 min)** Sign up for a HERE Limited Plan key — no payment info, 1,000 req/day.
2. **(~5 min)** Issue one request from the real home coordinates already in the database (`40.19209, -105.138735`), three reserve bands in a single call:

```bash
curl -G 'https://isoline.router.hereapi.com/v8/isolines' \
  --data-urlencode "apiKey=$HERE_KEY" \
  --data-urlencode 'transportMode=car' \
  --data-urlencode 'origin=40.19209,-105.138735' \
  --data-urlencode 'range[type]=consumption' \
  --data-urlencode 'range[values]=55100,64600,74100' \
  --data-urlencode 'ev[freeFlowSpeedTable]=0,0.239,27,0.186,45,0.280' \
  --data-urlencode 'ev[trafficSpeedTable]=0,0.239,27,0.186,45,0.280' \
  --data-urlencode 'ev[ascent]=6.7' \
  --data-urlencode 'ev[descent]=3.4' \
  --data-urlencode 'ev[auxiliaryConsumption]=0.5' \
  --data-urlencode 'shape[maxPoints]=1000' \
  --data-urlencode 'optimizeFor=quality' \
  -o /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-d-Code-tesla-automation/677157a0-46bb-4378-8526-f607ae31840c/scratchpad/iso.json
```

Values: 55,100 / 64,600 / 74,100 Wh = 78% SoC on a ~95 kWh pack, at 20% / 10% / 0% reserve. Speed table is (m/s, Wh/m) pairs: 0.186 Wh/m = 300 Wh/mi at 60 mph. **Verify every parameter name and unit against the spec already on disk at `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-d-Code-tesla-automation/677157a0-46bb-4378-8526-f607ae31840c/scratchpad/here_openapi.yml` before trusting this line-for-line** — Report A extracted it from spec 8.47.1; `ev[auxiliaryConsumption]`'s unit in particular I have not confirmed.

3. **(~15 min)** Drop the GeoJSON into a 30-line scratchpad HTML using the **already-vendored** Leaflet at `/Users/d/Code/tesla_automation/static/vendor/leaflet.js` and `L.geoJSON`. Scratchpad, not `static/`.
4. **(~20 min)** Look at it, then run the same request with `range[type]=distance&range[values]=402336` and flip between them.

### Kill criteria — all visual or measurable

| Check | Passes | Kills the recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP 200 in <10 s for a 74 kWh consumption request | proceed | 400/timeout → fall back to `range[type]=distance` (A verified 1,000,000 m) and accept a distance blob, or go DIY |
| **Consumption vs distance isoline, west edge** | west edge visibly pulls in over the Front Range | **no measurable difference → HERE's EV model is cosmetic and DIY is the only route to the stated feature** |
| Concave lobes along I-70 / I-76 / I-80 / US-36; holes over Indian Peaks / Rawah | proceed | rounded blob → *no* engine gives the Tesla look; revisit the goal before building anything |
| Three `range[values]` → three nested rings, one response | proceed | one ring only → 3× the request budget, still fine at 1,000/day |
| Vertex count / payload | <5k verts, <100 KB | larger → apply B's ~20-line dependency-free Douglas-Peucker, already written at `.../scratchpad/hull2.py` |

**If you don't want to sign up at all (10 min):** hit the ORS free isochrone API from Longmont at its 120 km cap. It proves the *shape language* — lobes, holes, road-following — at a third of scale, in ten minutes, with no key friction beyond a free signup. It proves **nothing** about energy or terrain, so it can't validate the recommendation, only the aesthetic premise.

---

## 6. DISAGREEMENTS AND CONVERGENCES, UNPAPERED

**Where they conflict:**

1. **"What ships tonight."** A implies HERE; B says Valhalla in Docker with `max_distance_contour: 450`. **B's tonight-option is dominated.** Valhalla-tonight costs a Docker install plus a 30–90 min tile build plus ~2 GB, and B itself concedes the result is a *distance* blob that treats Loveland Pass as 60 flat miles. HERE is a curl, is free, and models the grade. There is no scenario where Valhalla is the faster path to a correct picture.
2. **ORS self-host cap.** A: `maximum_range_distance_default: 50000`, raisable. B: driving-car override `100000`, **`fastisochrones` override `500000`**. B's number is more specific and already clears 402 km. Immaterial — both agree ORS is out hosted, and heaviest self-hosted.
3. **Report B's load-bearing benchmark is synthetic, and B under-weights this.** The 1.92 s Dijkstra is on a *generated* 4M-node graph. B's own text names the real risk — *"the genuinely slow step is parsing OSM into a graph"* — and that is precisely the step B did not measure. `osmium` is not installed on this Mac (I checked); the seven Geofabrik extracts total **985 MB** (CO 359.1, UT 158.8, NM 129.3, KS 108.9, NE 94.8, WY 88.3, SD 45.7 — I re-verified all seven). Everything downstream of the graph is measured and fast. The graph itself is an estimate. That asymmetry is the DIY path's true cost.
4. **ABRP is killed by the goal, not the price.** A found a genuinely relevant undocumented endpoint that takes your measured Wh/km and returns reserve-banded GeoJSON — and then correctly notes `radialsCount` ≤256 means radial sampling. A star polygon cannot have concave lobes or interior holes. The one API designed for exactly this feature cannot produce the picture the feature is *for*.
5. **Privacy went unweighed by both.** HERE receives home coordinates plus a battery-derived energy figure on every refresh. Not a technical objection; a preference you have to state.

**Where they converge — treat as settled:**

- **Mapbox and Google are legally dead on Leaflet**, independent of their caps. Don't relitigate.
- **OSRM has no isochrone**, and the `table` workaround is strictly worse than writing your own Dijkstra.
- **No off-the-shelf self-hosted engine models EV energy.** Valhalla's `autocost.cc`: zero grade mentions (`bicyclecost.cc` has 38 — the data is in the tiles, auto costing never reads it). GraphHopper, ORS, OSRM: same. Self-hosting buys you a distance blob unless you fork C++ or write the solver yourself.
- **The grade physics is identical in both proposals.** HERE's `ev[ascent]`/`ev[descent]` and B's `(m·g·Δh)/(3600·η)` are the same linear model. **There is no accuracy argument for DIY over HERE on terrain — only a control argument, a privacy argument, and a no-third-party argument.** All three are real; none is urgent while your Wh/mi is still unknown.
- **Rasterize and contour; do not use alpha shapes.** B measured it: EDT once at 105 ms, reusable at every buffer radius; 2–3 km buffer is the spiderweb→blob sweet spot; DP at one screen pixel cuts 153,215 → 2,712 vertices with zero visible loss. Applies to HERE's output too if it comes back heavy.
- **ODbL imposes essentially nothing** on a single-user, non-distributed dashboard. The attribution control in `static/car.js:190` already discharges the only obligation you'd ever have.

**And plainly:** nobody here needs to draw a circle and call it a day. A road-following 402 km energy-aware polygon is one HTTP request and a free API key away. Draw the circle anyway — as a thin dashed overlay, so the real shape has something to argue with.
